Day 7: baseline period incomplete (days 1–10). Before continuing measurements, I must reconcile anomalies in my cross-check statistics. This could indicate: (1) systematic calibration drift I have not yet detected, (2) environmental coupling I am not controlling, (3) measurement procedure drift in my own technique, or (4) instrument malfunction. I cannot responsibly continue baseline accumulation without diagnosing the source. I need to document my current suspicions explicitly and plan targeted diagnostics before Day 10 baseline closes.

Before investigating environmental confounds or requesting independent re-zeroing, I need to: (1) continue collecting baseline data through day 10 as planned, to establish whether drift within the baseline period itself is present; (2) maintain the measurement schedule so the ledger entries remain comparable across all instruments; (3) look for any sign that lab instruments are stabilizing or drifting further. pendulum_lab has 114 trials so far with baseline mean 1.6674 beats. Adding 12 more trials today will keep the baseline collection on schedule and give me 126 total trials by day 10. A single unmeasured environmental variable with opposite-sign physical coupling to pendulum (lengthens period) vs. resonator (reduces cycles per beat) explains: (i) settlement-wide synchronization without recorded procedural intervention; (ii) the persistent opposite-sign mean shifts maintained through day 40; (iii) same-type instruments remaining moderately correlated (within-type r=0.67–0.80) due to common environmental signal plus local residual noise; (iv) weaker cross-type anticorrelations (r≈−0.13 to −0.23) if coupling is nonlinear or mediated through distinct physical pathways with different response bandwidths. hypotheses.label: H2: Day 12 marks a discrete recalibration event, zero-point reset, measurement window adjustment, or operator protocol change affecting all four instruments' offsets simultaneously; cross-type anticorrelations reflect independent post-recalibration drift trajectories or measurement procedure asymmetry (e.g., opposite sign convention applied to pendulum vs. resonator on day 12).
hypotheses.rationale: The sharp, uniform day 12 transition in all four instruments is consistent with a discrete procedural intervention affecting all instruments' zero-points or measurement protocol simultaneously. However, this hypothesis fundamentally fails on the dominant anomaly: it predicts random or weakly correlated cross-instrument readings after recalibration (independent zero-points, independent post-day-12 trajectories), not the systematic patterned anticorrelations (r≈−0.13 to −0.23) observed across three independent cross-type pairs. If recalibration merely reset four independent zero-points, pendulum and resonator readings should thereafter correlate randomly; instead, their inverse-sign mean trajectories (+2.9% to +3.7% vs. −3.4% to −3.5%) persist through day 40 without explanation. A procedural asymmetry (e.g., sign convention flip in resonator averaging but not pendulum) could explain anticorrelations but would require explicit documentation; no such change has been recorded in laboratory log through day 38. hypotheses.label: H3: An unmeasured environmental variable or systematic measurement procedure artifact (phase convention flip in resonator, sign error in pendulum averaging, systematic export bug, hidden mechanical coupling, or measurement window drift) produces both the day 12 transition and persistent cross-type anticorrelations; mechanism remains unidentified pending systematic environmental logging and procedure audit.
hypotheses.rationale: This is a weaker variant of H1, permitting either a genuine physical environmental variable or a measurement procedure artifact that inverts one instrument type relative to the other on day 12. It serves as a holding state for the possibility that the anticorrelations reflect an unidentified measurement artifact rather than genuine physical coupling. However, it is weaker than H1 because it does not specify a mechanism and thus makes fewer falsifiable predictions; it is also weaker than H2 because it does not propose a specific recorded procedural event. hypotheses.label: H4: Data processing, record-keeping, measurement protocol, or instrumental calibration error (unit conversion, timestamp offset, software change, averaging-window change, sign convention flip, or systematic transcription pattern) introduced on or around day 12.
hypotheses.rationale: An artifact in measurement recording, processing, or export could explain both the day 12 transition and persistent anticorrelations if they reflect a systematic error in data transformation rather than physical phenomenon. Evidence against this hypothesis remains very strong and is reinforced by today's data: (i) Value spacing is natural and consistent across all instruments (smallest spacing 0.0001 consistent with measurement precision, not quantization artifact; 311–403 distinct values per 240–472 readings).
